title: What a Desired Market Is
lede: Some markets are easy to sell to and pay well. Most are not. The difference is visible before you send a single message, if you know what to look for.
deliverable: They leave with one candidate market scored against five tests, and a clear answer on whether to pursue it or move on.
body:
This lesson stops you wasting your first three months. People pick a market because they know someone in it, or because it sounds interesting, and then spend a quarter discovering nobody there has money or pain. A desired market is one where the maths already works before you arrive. Here is how to find one on purpose.

What makes a market desired

A desired market passes five tests. Not three out of five. All five. Each one you skip costs you a specific kind of grief later.

1. THEY ALREADY SPEND ON THE PROBLEM

The best signal that a market will pay you is that it is already paying someone. A part time admin. A $13k a year platform. A call answering service. An agency on retainer. Existing spend proves two things at once: the problem is real enough to pay for, and the money is already in the budget. You are not asking for new money. You are redirecting money that is already leaving.

2. THE PAIN HAS A DOLLAR FIGURE

You learned in the last two lessons that money is the final unit. A desired market is one where you can get to the dollars in one conversation. Missed calls times job value. Jobs turned away times margin. Wages on removable work. If the pain only ever converts to "it's frustrating", the market is not desired, however much they complain.

3. THEY HAVE THE MONEY

Pain without budget is charity work. Look for businesses with real revenue, real staff, and real overhead. A rough tell: if they employ people and own equipment or premises, a five figure system that removes a wage is a normal decision for them. If they are a solo operator doing $90k a year, it is not, no matter how much they like you.

4. THE DECISION MAKER IS REACHABLE

You need to be able to find the owner or operations lead and get a reply within a reasonable number of attempts. Trades, construction, clinics, agencies, distributors: owners answer their phones and their DMs. Enterprise and government: the person you reach is never the person who decides. Reachability is the difference between a thirty day sales cycle and a nine month one.

5. A HUMAN IS DOING WORK A SYSTEM COULD DO

This is the one that makes AI the obvious answer rather than a nice to have. Someone in the business is manually chasing, re-entering, reminding, answering, scheduling or reporting. That person's hours are the thing you remove, and that is where your price comes from. If the work is already automated well, you are not needed. If it is genuinely human judgement, you cannot replace it. The sweet spot is repeatable work done by a person because nobody built the system yet.

Score a candidate market

Do this on paper for every market you are considering. Score each test from 1 to 5, where 5 means strong evidence and 1 means you are guessing or the answer is no. Be honest. A 3 that should be a 1 costs you months.

TestWhat a 5 looks likeWhat a 1 looks likeYour score
Already spendPaying staff or software for this exact problem today."They'd probably pay if they saw the value."
Pain in dollarsYou can write the annual cost in one line.The pain is "annoying" or "messy".
Ability to payMultiple staff, equipment, premises, steady revenue.Solo operators, early stage, cash tight.
Decision maker reachableOwner's name and direct line findable in minutes.Procurement, committees, "send it to info@".
Human doing system workNamed person spends hours a week on repeatable admin.Already automated, or the work needs expert judgement.

A total of 20 or more is a desired market. Go. Between 15 and 19, find out which test is dragging and whether a narrower segment fixes it (often "construction" scores 16 and "high ticket residential builders with five plus staff" scores 22). Under 15, move on without guilt. The market is not wrong, it is just not yours.

An illustrative scoring. Candidate: residential builders doing larger jobs, five to thirty staff. Already spend: they run a CRM and employ office admin, score 5. Pain in dollars: admin wage plus platform fees plus turned away jobs, easy to write down, score 5. Ability to pay: equipment, crews, six and seven figure revenue, score 5. Decision maker: the owner is on site, on the phone, on Instagram, score 4. Human doing system work: the admin chasing sign offs and re-entering quotes, score 5. Total 24. That is a desired market, and it is the shape of the market behind the $22k CRM deal in Module 6. Compare it to "small cafes" which score roughly 2, 2, 1, 4, 3. Lovely people, not a market for five figure systems.

How you capitalise on it

Finding a desired market is half the lesson. The other half is what happens when you commit to one, because a desired market rewards focus in a way a scattered approach never will.

You become the specialist. The owner who hears "we build systems for residential builders" trusts you before you have said anything else, because you sound like you have seen their problem before. The one who hears "we do AI for businesses" has to be convinced you understand theirs. Specialists charge more and sell faster for the same work.

Your demo compounds. Build one demo for a builder and it works, with light changes, for the next fifty builders. Build one for a builder, one for a dentist and one for a gym and you have three half finished demos and no proof. Every deal in a desired market makes the next demo better and the next proposal faster.

Your proof compounds. One case study in a niche is worth more than ten across random industries, because the prospect sees themselves in it. "We removed $78k of admin cost for a builder in Brisbane" lands with every builder who hears it. The second and third cases make you the obvious choice before the call starts.

Your outreach gets simpler. One list. One message, adapted per channel. One set of objections you have heard before. The acquisition system in Module 3 is built to run on exactly this: a defined market, a defined pain, a defined buyer. Spread across five markets, it falls apart.

The counter argument you will feel is "but I'm limiting myself". You are not. There are tens of thousands of businesses in any decent niche. You will not run out. What you are limiting is how many different problems you have to understand at once, and that is the thing that keeps beginners stuck.

What Jarvis does here

Jarvis can run the five tests on a candidate market from a few inputs and tell you where the weak spot is. Use it to compare three or four candidates in one sitting instead of agonising over one.

Score this candidate market as a high ticket AI services target. Market: [describe it: industry, size of business, location]. The problem I think I can solve: [one sentence]. What I know about who does that work today: [staff, software, outsourced, unknown]. Score each of these five tests from 1 to 5 with one line of reasoning each: they already spend on the problem, the pain has a dollar figure, they have the money, the decision maker is reachable, a human is doing work a system could do. Give a total out of 25. If any test scores 3 or below, suggest a narrower segment of the same market that would score higher, and say what evidence I would need to confirm it. Do not flatter the market. If it is weak, say so.

Do this now

Pick your single strongest candidate market and score it on the table above, by hand, before you ask Jarvis. Then run the prompt and compare. Where you and Jarvis disagree, that is the test you need to go and check in the real world this week: three phone calls or three DMs to owners in that market, asking who handles the work today and what it costs them.

Bring the scored table to your weekly group strategy session. We pick the market together before you build a demo for it. Choosing the market is the decision that everything after it depends on, so it is the one we do not rush.
